introduction: Fair warning. This is an embellished fictional dramatization that may or may not be based on true stories. The narrator is a guy named Charlie Hack, and any resemblance to me is mostly coincidental. Names, characters, companies and events are fictitious, or used fictitiously.
This preview drops you into the middle of the book. Part Three. It's called C Things That Looked Like A Things.

Silicon Valley is very good at telling a story about A players. The people who look like they were always going to win, and the companies that look like they were always going to work. The myth is a straight line: a garage, a genius, a ticker symbol. But most of the real work looks nothing like that. It looks like another ordinary Tuesday, doing the next right thing.
And from the outside, a C thing can look like an A thing. The applause is loud, and the real work is quieter. This book is about that gap, between what people saw and what was really going on.

A C player is not a failure. It's the person who was never the smartest in the room, and kept going anyway. Because there is always the smarter guy in the room. The richer guy, the more experienced, the wisest. The better father, the better brother, the better sister, the better daughter.

Greg Glassman noticed that the fittest person on earth might rank only in the 75th percentile at any single event. Good at everything beats best at one thing. That's a C player, and it's why C players, the ones who keep stacking fundamentals and never stop, end up outlasting the A players.

The Valley falls in love with products. Specific wins, in specific years. I got more out of building a platform: a foundation you can stand on, then build the next thing on, and the thing after that. You don't invent a career in one move. You stack building blocks: habits, fundamentals, the unglamorous layer nobody puts on a slide. That layer is what you actually stand on later.
It's all relative, how good you look from the outside. But one thing stayed for certain. I just kept going. And I kept doing my best.

Then the work itself changed. I'm usually the most excited person in the room about AI. Which is funny, because I should be the saddest. Because AI came after the code writers first. In my own work, AI now writes essentially all of the code I ship. That's how I work. Not a measured team result. Not a general industry figure.

Software engineering was never about writing code. Writing code was just the tedious part you had to do to build your ideas. It's about solving big problems with abstraction. Each part is just data in, some logic, and data out. Abstraction is key. You climb down the ladder, and you climb back up.

So software engineering practices have to be geared around that. That's what Software Engineering 101 and 201 are about, and it's the second half of this book: how to work now, and how companies should use AI.

The book begins with a green-screen dream, and it ends by dreaming about AI. This part, in the middle, is the turn. It's free. It's open. And when version one is ready, if you were around for any of it, you get to tell your side. The story is still being written.

chapters.title: Building Blocks
chapters.subtitle: How a result I never set as a goal came out of stacked foundations
chapters.summary: A nonfiction interlude in Clark Huang's own voice: his fitness journey from a 2018 wake-up through Orangetheory, CrossFit, gymnastics skills like the hollow hold, the ring muscle-up, and double unders, a triathlon ladder from sprint to Olympic to half, and six official marathons, including a 3:03:55 Boston qualifier at 47 that he never set as a goal when he started. A full Ironman is something he looks forward to. Progressive overload, told through the legend of Milo of Croton, sits with the weightlifting. The result came out of stacked foundations. He still calls himself a C player in CrossFit. A light turn toward Chapter 36, on how companies should use AI, closes the chapter.
chapters.rule: Build the foundation, not the number. Learn the next step when you need it. Practice the core movements until they are yours, then put them in combination. Keep going. Let the result emerge from the work you stacked, and measure the work you actually did. The same rule holds in life, in tech, in marketing, and in finance: if the foundation is weak, nothing lasting gets built. When you later apply AI to that work, put it on fundamentals you already understand.

thesis.text: I build platforms and models, not products or specific numbers. Weak foundations in life, tech, marketing, or finance mean nothing lasting gets built.

chapters.title: Sick, Well, Fit
chapters.subtitle: How companies should use AI: train to be fit, not just well
chapters.summary: Clark Huang's view is that AI is far more powerful in the hands of people who understand the fundamentals of the area they apply it to than for someone vibing their way in, and this chapter gives that view a picture: Greg Glassman's line from sickness through wellness to fitness. Most companies aim for well, a normal reading; fit is a margin, and making AI part of how a company operates is hard enough to need one. The chapter carries CrossFit's models over to a company one by one (markers, the hopper, three engines, work capacity, mechanics then consistency then intensity, the pyramid, virtuosity, benchmarks, scaling, luck, open scoring) and ends with "Business Fitness in 100 Words" and a rule a person or an agent can follow.
chapters.rule: Well is a reading and fit is a margin, so train for fit. Choose markers you can observe, time the same work every quarter, and practice the event you dread. Put AI on fundamentals you understand: mechanics first, then consistency, and only then intensity. In full: when you report how a team, a system, or an agent’s work is doing, do not start with a feeling. Name the markers, give each a reading of sick, well, or fit, and show evidence someone else can check. If one marker is moving the wrong way while the others improve, say that first, and investigate it first. Before you start a plan, write down the measurement you expect, and afterward say whether it came true. Keep a short list of benchmark work, hold the work the same, time it every quarter, and post the times. Name the event you least want to draw, and rehearse it. Turn AI, scope, or speed up only where three things hold: someone understands the fundamentals well enough to tell when the output is wrong; the mechanics are right; and the result passes the same check without a hero. Scale the load to the size of the team and keep the movement. Plan the slack. Fitness improves the odds. It does not remove bad luck.

thesis.text: I strongly believe that AI is even more powerful to those that actually understand the fundamentals of the area they are applying AI to. Orders of magnitude more than the person vibing their way into a discipline AI gives them access to.

featured.title: Business Fitness in 100 Words
featured.text: Spend on customers and product, people and tools, a little on overhead, nothing on vanity. Keep cash at levels that fund growth but not waste. Practice the core movements: build, sell, serve, collect. Master the basics: clean data, clear owners, written decisions, honest numbers. Ship, test, learn and fix, hard and fast. Every week, mix these in as many combinations as the work demands. Routine is the enemy; process is not. Keep projects short and intense. Put AI in every movement, mechanics first. Regularly take on problems you've never seen. Measure it, or it didn't happen.
featured.adapted_from: Greg Glassman, “World-Class Fitness in 100 Words,” CrossFit Journal, October 2002: https://library.crossfit.com/free/pdf/CFJ-trial.pdf
featured.score_prompt: Read "Business Fitness in 100 Words" in https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/chapters/36-sick-well-fit/index.md (Chapter 36 of Clark Huang's free OpenBook, Silicon Valley C Players). Then score my company, or my team, against it, one line at a time. For each line: is it sick, well, or fit, and what evidence would prove that? Interview me one question at a time before you score; do not invent facts about my company. Finish with the two lines to work on first, one benchmark I could time every quarter, and the event I would least like to see come out of the hopper.

stories.title: I built the app. Would people use it every month?
